readings.title: Why getting your hands dirty is good for you
body: 5 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Becca Warner Putting our hands in soil and touching grass, trees or moss provides a wide range of health benefits, for our skin and wider immune system. I take a long walk in my nearest park every day, almost religiously. There are plenty of different tree species to look at, an everchanging cast of fragrant flowers in spring, and enthusiastic birdsong fills the air. But the sensory experience usually stops there. However mucky my shoes get, I usually come home with clean hands. Research, though, suggests there's something to be said for reaching out to touch the trees, shrubs and soil I usually walk past. Mira Grönroos, an ecologist and nature-health researcher at the Finnish Environment Institute, asked people to rub their hands with soil, peat and moss for 20 seconds as part of an experiment . She found that the abundance and variety of microbes on their skin increased, even after they rinsed their hands with tap water. "To the naked eye [their hands] looked clean," she says, "but the change was so huge". The idea of more bacteria on our skin might not sound appealing. But when there's a rich mix of microbes living alongside each other, they keep each other in check and defend us against more harmful, pathogenic bacteria . A growing body of research shows that contact with natural materials, like soil and plants, is an easy way to boost our skin's microbial diversity , and that this not only benefits our skin, but also our immune system. Twenty seconds isn't long – I'd happily pause on my walk to touch some tree bark or sit down in the grass. But more would be much better, Grönroos says, as in her experiment "the skin microbiota very quickly returned to a similar state as it was before". The results suggest that prolonged or frequent skin contact with nature could significantly change what's happening on our skin and in our bodies.   Mucky hands are the norm for children at Aurinkolinna daycare centre in central Finland. They spend at least a couple of hours every day playing outside in a wooded playground, racing between bushes and trees, climbing ropes, making sandcastles, splashing in puddles and grabbing fistfuls of dirt and woodchips. By the end of each day they are covered head to toe in mud. Scientists are now studying how this could be good for their health. By analysing microbes on the children's skin, saliva and faeces, alongside blood and hair samples, researchers are learning what happens to their immune systems over a three-year period when nature is brought into the yards where they play every day. Aurinkolinna is one of 43 daycare centres in Finland taking part in the Vahvistu research project , which builds on a recent two-year study led by environmental scientist Marja Roslund. In 2016-17, she brought the forest floor into a daycare yard – complete with peat and planting boxes – and measured the impact on young children's skin, saliva and gut bacteria after they had played there regularly for 28 days, and again after a year. Compared to children who played in a paved yard, those on the forest floor had greater microbial diversity on their skin a year later. This diversity is important for the health of our skin. Increasing the diversity of bacteria on the skin can prevent disease-causing bacteria from becoming dominant, keeping the microbial community in balance, Roslund says. "Disease is like a dictator, and healthy skin is like a democracy."  Roslund's research found fewer potential pathogens on children's skin when they had played on the forest floor, likely because the number and diversity of other microbes crowds out these "bad" bacteria. "Because there is so much of everything else, there is not so much space for the pathogens," she says. Taking care of our skin also has benefits that run much deeper. Skin health can impact hormonal activity , cardiovascular disease , and even cognitive function . In particular, research is starting to show that exposing our skin to diverse bacteria can impact our immune system .  Roslund asked a group of young children to play in a sandbox enriched with microbially diverse soil, while another group played in a sandbox that looked the same but contained less microbial diversity. As we might expect, the diversity of certain bacteria on children's skin increased when they played in the microbially rich sandbox. But there were also changes to the immune markers, called cytokines, in these children's blood samples that support immunoregulation – the immune system's ability to fight off threats without becoming overactive. It is these and similar findings that inspired the Vahvistu project. At Aurinkolinna, government funding has helped transform the yard so it now includes woodchips instead of gravel, a bigger sanded area, and wooden pathways, alongside the birch and pine trees that were already there. The research behind the Vahvistu project supports what is known as the biodiversity hypothesis – the idea that air, plants and soil rich in diverse microbes have an important influence on the human microbiome, and therefore our health. It has long been suggested that the loss of biodiversity in our environment could be behind the current rise in immune-related conditions, and Roslund's research may help to explain how and why that is. She found that one family of bacteria, namely gammaproteobacteria, plays a particularly important role. Gammaproteobacterial diversity increased on children's skin when they played in the yard with the forest floor, and this increase was associated with more regulatory T cells – white blood cells that help control and balance the immune system and are important for preventing autoimmune diseases, she says. For now, it's not clear exactly what this means for immune-mediated diseases like eczema, asthma or allergies. "We cannot yet say that when you have contact with nature, you will not get asthma, for example. But it seems that it might reduce the possibility of getting those immune system disorders," Grönroos says.   These health benefits aren't only seen in children. In one study, adults were asked to grow vegetables indoors over winter, some using microbially diverse soil and others using similar-looking but microbially poor soil. They tended to the plants every day for a month and ate their crops. Those using the microbially-diverse soil saw an increase in the diversity of bacteria on their skin, and on the number of anti-inflammatory cytokines in their blood – while the other group didn't. When I go outdoors with my children, if they want to pick some cones or sticks, I don't say 'no'. I let them bring them home and play there – Mira Grönroos This kind of gardening "is a good example of an easily accessible way of nature contact, and it was quite surprising that this kind of exposure really showed changes in the immune system functioning", Grönroos says.  In another study, researchers installed "green walls" made of living plants in Finnish offices and measured the effect on workers after two weeks. They found that the diversity of microbes on their skin increased, and levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in their blood went down. They also saw an increase in Lactobacillus microbes on their skin, which is  important for skin health .   More like this: •  Four benefits of going out in the rain •  Want a better night's sleep? Go camping •  What watching the sunset really does for your health   Grönroos puts her findings into practice with her own family. "When I go outdoors with my children, if they want to pick some cones or sticks, I don't say 'no' to them. I let them bring them home and play there." We should start applying this thinking to our cities, Grönroos adds. "[Cities] should be built so that citizens are able to get into contact with nature. It would be good if some of that contact was unintentional, so people wouldn't need to decide to go there, they would come into contact with nature on their way to work or school," she says. There's more for science to discover about exactly how contact with nature impacts the immune system, but for Grönroos, the findings so far are enough to make the grubby hands and muddy carpet worth it. "It's low risk," she says, with "lots of potential benefits without any obvious major harms." These findings are, perhaps, a reminder to us all to reach out and touch that mossy tree, to sit down in the grass – to not be afraid of a bit of mud. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . 5天前 分享 保存 在Google上添加为首选 Becca Warner 把手伸进泥土，触摸草地、树木或苔藓，能为我们的皮肤和更广泛的免疫系统带来诸多健康益处。我几乎每天都会去最近的公园长时间散步，近乎虔诚。那里有众多不同种类的树木可供观赏，春天还有不断变换的芬芳花朵，空气中充满了热情的鸟鸣。但感官体验通常止步于此。无论我的鞋子变得多脏，我回家时双手通常是干净的。然而，研究表明，伸手去触摸我通常路过时视而不见的树木、灌木和土壤，是有其道理的。芬兰环境研究所的生态学家兼自然健康研究员米拉·格伦罗斯在一项实验中要求人们用土壤、泥炭和苔藓搓手20秒。她发现，即使他们用自来水冲洗双手后，皮肤上微生物的丰富度和多样性仍然增加了。“肉眼看去[他们的手]是干净的，”她说，“但变化是如此巨大。”皮肤上有更多细菌的想法听起来可能并不吸引人。但当大量微生物共同生存时，它们会相互制约，并保护我们免受更有害的病原菌侵袭。越来越多的研究表明，接触土壤和植物等自然物质是提升皮肤微生物多样性的简便方法，而这不仅有益于我们的皮肤，也有益于我们的免疫系统。20秒并不长——我很乐意在散步时停下来触摸一些树皮，或者坐在草地上。但格伦罗斯说，接触更多会好得多，因为在她实验中“皮肤微生物群很快就恢复到与之前相似的状态”。研究结果表明，长时间或频繁地与自然进行皮肤接触，可能会显著改变我们皮肤上和体内的状况。在芬兰中部的奥林科林纳日托中心，脏手是孩子们的常态。他们每天至少有几个小时在树林里的游乐场户外玩耍，在灌木和树木之间奔跑，攀爬绳索，堆沙堡，在水坑里踩水，抓起一把把泥土和木屑。每天结束时，他们从头到脚都沾满泥巴。科学家们现在正在研究这可能如何有益于他们的健康。通过分析孩子们皮肤、唾液和粪便中的微生物，以及血液和头发样本，研究人员正在了解当自然被引入他们每天玩耍的院子后，他们的免疫系统在三年期间会发生什么变化。奥林科林纳是芬兰43个参与Vahvistu研究项目的日托中心之一，该项目建立在环境科学家玛丽亚·罗斯隆德最近领导的一项为期两年的研究基础上。在2

##段落
016-17年，她把森林地表搬进了日托中心的院子——连同泥炭和种植箱——并测量了幼儿在此定期玩耍28天后，以及一年后，其皮肤、唾液和肠道细菌受到的影响。与在铺砌院子里玩耍的孩子相比，一年后，在森林地表玩耍的孩子皮肤上的微生物多样性更高。这种多样性对我们皮肤的健康很重要。罗斯伦德说，增加皮肤上细菌的多样性可以防止致病细菌占据主导地位，从而保持微生物群落的平衡。“疾病就像独裁者，而健康的皮肤就像民主。”罗斯伦德的研究发现，当孩子们在森林地表玩耍时，他们皮肤上的潜在病原体更少，这可能是因为其他微生物的数量和多样性挤占了这些“坏”细菌。“因为其他东西太多了，病原体就没有那么多空间了，”她说。呵护我们的皮肤还有更深远的好处。皮肤健康会影响激素活动、心血管疾病，甚至认知功能。尤其是，研究开始表明，让我们的皮肤接触多样的细菌可以影响我们的免疫系统。罗斯伦德让一组幼儿在一个富含微生物多样性土壤的沙坑里玩耍，而另一组则在一个看起来相同但微生物多样性较低的沙坑里玩耍。正如我们可能预料的那样，当孩子们在微生物丰富的沙坑里玩耍时，他们皮肤上某些细菌的多样性增加了。但这些孩子血样中被称为细胞因子的免疫标志物也发生了变化，这些变化支持免疫调节——即免疫系统在不变得过度活跃的情况下抵御威胁的能力。正是这些以及类似的发现启发了Vahvistu项目。在Aurinkolinna，政府资金帮助改造了院子，现在它包括木屑而不是砾石、更大的沙地以及木制小径，还有原本就有的桦树和松树。Vahvistu项目背后的研究支持所谓的生物多样性假说——即富含多样微生物的空气、植物和土壤对人体微生物组，进而对我们的健康有重要影响。长期以来，人们一直认为环境中生物多样性的丧失可能是当前免疫相关疾病增加的原因，而罗斯伦德的研究可能有助于解释这是如何以及为何发生的。她发现，一个细菌家族，即γ-变形菌纲，起着特别重要的作用。当孩子们在带有森林地表的院子里玩耍时，他们皮肤上的γ-变形菌纲多样性增加了，而这种增加与更多的调节

## 调节性T细胞——她表示，这是一种有助于控制和平衡免疫系统的白细胞，对预防自身免疫性疾病很重要。目前尚不清楚这对湿疹、哮喘或过敏等免疫介导疾病究竟意味着什么。“例如，我们还不能说你接触自然就不会得哮喘。但似乎它可能会降低患上这些免疫系统疾病的可能性，”格伦罗斯说。

## 这些健康益处不仅仅体现在儿童身上。在一项研究中，成年人被要求在冬季于室内种植蔬菜，一些人使用微生物多样化的土壤，另一些人则使用外观相似但微生物贫乏的土壤。他们每天照料植物，持续一个月，并食用自己的收成。使用微生物多样化土壤的那组人，皮肤上细菌的多样性有所增加，血液中抗炎细胞因子的数量也有所增加——而另一组则没有变化。

## 当我带孩子们去户外时，如果他们想捡一些松果或树枝，我不会说“不行”。我让他们带回家玩——米拉·格伦罗斯

## 格伦罗斯说，这种园艺“是一个很好的例子，说明了一种容易实现的接触自然的方式，而且相当令人惊讶的是，这种接触确实显示了免疫系统功能的改变”。

## 在另一项研究中，研究人员在芬兰的办公室里安装了由活体植物构成的“绿墙”，并在两周后测量了对员工的影响。他们发现员工皮肤上微生物的多样性增加了，血液中促炎细胞因子的水平下降了。他们还发现皮肤上乳酸杆菌微生物有所增加，这对皮肤健康很重要。

## 格伦罗斯将这些研究发现付诸自己的家庭实践。“当我带孩子们去户外时，如果他们想捡一些松果或树枝，我不会对他们说‘不行’。我让他们带回家玩。”

## 格伦罗斯补充说，我们应该开始将这种思路应用到城市建设中。“（城市）的规划应该让市民能够接触自然。如果其中一些接触是无意间的，那就更好了，这样人们就不需要有意识地去那里，他们会在上班或上学的路上接触到自然，”她说。

## 关于接触自然究竟如何影响免疫系统，还有更多有待科学发现，但对格伦罗斯来说，目前的研究结果足以让那些脏兮兮的手和沾满泥巴的地毯变得值得。“风险很低，”她说，“有大量潜在益处，却没有明显的重大危害。”

readings.title: Is Italy the new tax haven for the global rich?
body: 22 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Italy has already been attacked by the French Government for using tax incentives to lure wealthy French and other international residents away, but with the war in the Middle East hurting the Gulf states, Italy has become an even more attractive location for the rich. Tax wasn't the main reason for leaving France, Robert insists over a café crème at Charles de Gaulle airport. It was the beauty of Italy, the bella vita  (the beautiful/good life), the art and the music. But for the Frenchman, buying a house in Rome and becoming an Italian tax resident was a very nice part of the package offered by the country, where high net worth individuals can pay a fixed annual tax on all foreign income – regardless of amount – and enjoy a series of other exemptions.  Robert, who describes himself as only "moderately wealthy", moved to Italy eight years ago after a career in computers which ended with him selling his company. Robert, not his real name, may not be among the French billionaires who have fled the French taxman for Italy, but the advantages to him are clear.   If he'd been buying a house in France, he would have had to pay what the French call frais de notaire (solicitor's fees) most of which goes to the government (much like Stamp Duty in the UK or Real Estate Transfer Taxes in the US). In Italy there's an exemption for the prima casa , the first house you buy. In France, President Macron transformed France's Impot sur la Fortune  (wealth tax) into an Impot sur la Fortune Immobilière  (real estate wealth tax) so stock market investments, for example, are no longer affected but "if you have ten million dollars' worth of property, this tax is very painful indeed," says Robert. Again, there's nothing like that in Italy.  In France you also have to pay a property tax ( taxe foncière or land tax). "We don't have that here for the prima casa (first home)," says Robert, although he notes "there is a high charge for refuse collection". The best thing as far as he is concerned is that there is no inheritance tax on property you own in Italy up to €1 million ($1.1 million) and it's only 4% beyond that threshold. In France the tax-free limit is much lower – €100,000 ($110,000) – and beyond that it's a sliding scale up to a top rate of 45%. But it's for the seriously rich that Italy starts to look like a fiscal paradise. "I have friends who have moved here for tax reasons and others who are thinking about it," Robert tells me. "For people who really pay a lot of tax, Italy is very attractive because of it's "flat tax". In Italy, the taxman fixes an upper limit of tax that can be levied on income. However much you earn, you never pay more than that. The upper limit is now €300,000 ($353,000). Although not long ago it was €100,000 before rising to €200,000. If you're paying a million euros of income tax a year in France, Italy is very tempting. As for US citizens, Americans are always taxable on worldwide income, so moving to Italy would not help their tax bill. Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe – Peter Ferrigno Robert tells me that he has two rich French friends who have moved to Italy in the past few months, but they came from the UK. They were both working in finance in the City of London and were keen to move to a place where the fiscal regime was as sympathetic to them as the one Britain had before it changed the rules for wealthy foreign residents.  "Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe. And it means you get tax certainty and clarity, within the heart of Europe, rather than having to go a long way," says Peter Ferrigno, director of tax services at wealth migration specialists Henley & Partners. "We have meetings with people every week who would like to leave France," says Paris-based tax lawyer Jerome Barre. "They are unhappy about the tax situation now and they are worried that it will become harsher in the future. People are not confident with the political climate. Taxes are changing a lot, almost every year. People are frightened that after the election of the new president in 2027, things could become harder than today," he says. At this stage though it's more "questions from entrepreneurs and wealthy people who are wondering if they would like to move or not move rather than people actually moving," Jerome Barre explains. "Relocation requires full commitment and careful structuring," he stresses. He adds that for business-owners  " they need to change the seat of the company. They are subject in France to an exit tax." If many wealthy French people are at the "thinking-about-moving" stage, the question is being felt even more acutely in the United Arab Emirates. It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE – Peter Ferrigno But giving up on Dubai's zero-tax regime will be very difficult for many. "When you are in a country where you do not pay any tax, it's very difficult to come back to a country where you have to pay a lot. Especially for those used to spending a lot of money. The net in your pocket is very different, says Barre. And, he adds, people who have grown used to the zero-tax life "are not used to administrative formalities anymore – tax returns, documents – so it's not easy." More like this: • Dubai's tourism industry reels from 'brutal' impact of war • Why more Americans are now moving to Ireland • Is New York's cannabis business really flying high? "It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE," says Henley & Partners' Peter Ferrigno. "But I think it's far too early for people to wholesale uproot their life when it involves work, family, etc. The vast majority of people in the UAE are still regular people doing regular jobs, even most of the millionaires are millionaires because they are doing well paid jobs rather than being asset owners. If the war is relatively short, they will remain. If it drags on, then people will inevitably look elsewhere, or relocate the family and work remotely until it's safer. If you're in the UAE for work, there aren't likely to be that many equivalent roles in Italy," he says. However, it is likely that the war in the Middle East will dissuade many rich Europeans who would have otherwise moved there from re-locating to the UAE. Last year, Dubai was the number one destination by far for migrating millionaires, according to Henley & Partners. That number is bound to tumble in 2026, and with its attractive offer for the very wealthy, as well as its reputation for  la dolce vita  of course, it may well be Italy that benefits. -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights.  For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . ##段落
2026年4月22日 分享 保存 在谷歌上添加为首选 约翰·劳伦森 意大利此前已因利用税收优惠吸引富裕的法国人及其他国际居民迁入，而遭到法国政府的抨击，但随着中东战争对海湾国家造成冲击，意大利对富人而言已变得更具吸引力。在戴高乐机场喝咖啡奶油时，罗伯特坚称，税收并非他离开法国的主要原因。真正的原因是意大利的美景、美好的生活、艺术与音乐。但对这位法国人来说，在罗马购置房产并成为意大利税务居民，是该国所提供的一揽子方案中极为诱人的一部分——在意大利，高净值个人可以就所有海外收入缴纳固定的年度税额，不论金额多少，并享受一系列其他豁免。罗伯特自称只是“中等富裕”，八年前在结束计算机行业的职业生涯并卖掉自己的公司后移居意大利。罗伯特并非真名，他或许不属于那些为躲避法国税务而逃往意大利的法国亿万富翁之列，但对他而言，好处显而易见。如果他是在法国买房，就必须支付法国人所说的“公证费”，其中大部分归政府所有（很像英国的印花税或美国的房地产转让税）。而在意大利，购买首套房可享受豁免。在法国，马克龙总统将法国的“财富税”改为“房地产财富税”，因此股票市场投资等不再受影响，但罗伯特说：“如果你拥有价值一千万美元的房产，这项税确实非常痛苦。”而在意大利，同样没有这类税。在法国，你还必须缴纳房产税（土地税）。“我们这里首套房不用交，”罗伯特说，不过他指出“垃圾收集费很高”。在他看来，最好的一点是，你在意大利拥有的房产价值不超过100万欧元（110万美元）时无需缴纳遗产税，超过这一门槛也只需缴纳4%。而在法国，免税限额要低得多——仅为10万欧元（11万美元）——超过部分则按累进税率征收，最高可达45%。但正是对真正的富豪而言，意大利才开始显得像一座税收天堂。“我有朋友因税务原因搬到这里，也有人在考虑这么做，”罗伯特告诉我。“对于真正缴纳大量税款的人来说，意大利因其‘单一税’而极具吸引力。”在意大利，税务部门对可征收的收入设定了税额上限。无论你赚多少，缴纳的税款都不会超过这个上限。目前这一上限为30万欧元（35.3万美元）。尽管

##段落
虽然不久前还是10万欧元，后来涨到了20万欧元。如果你在法国每年缴纳100万欧元的所得税，意大利就非常有吸引力。至于美国公民，美国人始终需要就其全球收入纳税，因此移居意大利并不会减轻他们的税负。即便税率高达30万欧元，对于年收入超过100万欧元的人来说，意大利的统一税率相比欧洲其他任何地方仍然很低——彼得·费里尼奥告诉我，他有两位富有的法国朋友在过去几个月里搬到了意大利，但他们是从英国来的。他们两人都在伦敦金融城从事金融工作，并且渴望搬到一个财政制度对他们友好的地方，就像英国在修改针对富裕外国居民的规则之前那样。

##段落
“即便税率高达30万欧元，对于年收入超过100万欧元的人来说，意大利的统一税率相比欧洲其他任何地方仍然很低。而且这意味着你可以在欧洲腹地获得税收的确定性和清晰度，而不必远走他乡，”财富移民专业机构Henley & Partners的税务服务总监彼得·费里尼奥表示。“我们每周都会与想要离开法国的人会面，”驻巴黎的税务律师杰罗姆·巴雷说。“他们对当前的税收状况感到不满，并且担心未来会变得更加严苛。人们对政治气候缺乏信心。税收变化很大，几乎每年都在变。人们担心2027年新总统选举之后，情况可能会比现在更加艰难，”他说。不过，杰罗姆·巴雷解释说，在现阶段，更多的是“企业家和富裕人士在思考自己是否想要搬迁，而不是人们实际已经在搬迁”。“搬迁需要全身心的投入和精心的规划，”他强调说。他补充说，对于企业主而言，“他们需要更换公司的注册地。他们在法国需要缴纳退出税。”

##段落
如果许多富有的法国人正处于“考虑搬迁”的阶段，那么在阿拉伯联合酋长国，这个问题被感受得更加深切。许多人重新考虑阿联酋是不可避免的——彼得·费里尼奥。但对许多人来说，放弃迪拜的零税制将非常困难。“当你身处一个不需要缴纳任何税收的国家时，要回到一个需要缴纳大量税收的国家是非常困难的。尤其是对于那些习惯了大手笔花钱的人来说。你口袋里的净收入差别很大，”巴雷说。他还补充说，那些已经习惯了零税生活的人“不再习惯行政手续——纳税申报、文件——所以并不容易。”更多类似内容：• 迪拜旅游业因战争的“残酷”冲击而动荡 • 为什么越来越多的美国人正在移居爱尔兰 • 纽约的大麻生意真的在腾飞吗

##段落
“很多人会重新考虑阿联酋，这是不可避免的，”Henley & Partners的彼得·费里尼奥表示。“但我认为，当涉及工作、家庭等因素时，人们现在就彻底连根拔起、迁走生活，还为时过早。阿联酋的绝大多数人仍然是做着普通工作的普通人，甚至大多数百万富翁之所以是百万富翁，是因为他们从事高薪工作，而不是因为他们是资产所有者。如果这场战争相对短暂，他们会留下来。如果战争拖下去，那么人们不可避免地会另寻他处，或者把家人迁走、远程工作，直到更安全为止。如果你是为了工作去阿联酋，意大利不太可能有那么多同等职位，”他说。然而，中东战争很可能会让许多原本会迁往那里的富有欧洲人打消迁居阿联酋的念头。根据Henley & Partners的数据，去年迪拜是迄今百万富翁迁移的首选目的地。这一数字在2026年势必大幅下滑，而凭借其对超级富豪的吸引力以及当然还有“甜蜜生活”的声誉，获益的很可能是意大利。——想获取面向董事会及更广泛决策层的全球洞察与专家分析，请订阅《World of Business》通讯，而《The Essential List》则精选推送专题文章与洞察。想了解更多商业及更多领域的内容，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业 国际商业 专题 商业世界

readings.title: 25 years after 9/11, the GOP has never been more anti-Muslim
body: Today, Explained newsletter 25 years after 9/11, the GOP has never been more anti-Muslim The GOP wants America to fear Muslims. by Cameron Peters Sep 11, 2026, 10:00 PM UTC Gift New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rudy Giuliani arrive ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum in Manhattan on September 11, 2026. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . Hi readers — today marks 25 years since 9/11. In New York City, Washington, and Pennsylvania, survivors, families, and politicians are gathering to grieve and commemorate the attacks. Today, we wanted to focus on one small part of the story in New York City, where former Mayor Rudy Giuliani singled out Mayor Zohran Mamdani , who is Muslim, with an Islamophobic screed about Mamdani’s participation in memorial ceremonies. Giuliani’s rant, to be clear, is not really news in its own right; 25 years on, he’s less “America’s mayor” than he is the twice - disbarred , disgraced former lawyer of President Donald Trump. (And Mamdani did attend the event, even shaking hands with Giuliani.) But Giuliani’s remarks are, unfortunately, emblematic of a disturbing trend in Republican politics, where open, aggressive Islamophobia is on the rise — 25 years after a particularly ugly brand of it emerged in response to 9/11. One major difference between then and now? In 2001, many politicians tried to tamp it down rather than inflame it. As Nathan Lean, an assistant teaching professor at North Carolina State University and author of the book The Islamophobia Industry , explained to my colleague Christian Paz last month : “Islamophobia has passed the dinner table test. You can say things about Muslims with basic impunity today. And it’s institutionalized in the way that prejudice that targets other marginalized communities is not.” Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. The 2026 midterm elections have provided a particularly clear showcase for the right’s Islamophobic turn. On Thursday, at the second and final night of the GOP’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) told attendees that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans. “They share the same enemies,” he said. “They hate Christians. They hate Jews. They hate capitalism. They hate the Constitution, and they hate America.” At another point in Cruz’s speech, attendees screamed “he should be shot” as Cruz name-checked Mamdani, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (who is Muslim, and who Cruz said “says he has an obligation to Sharia Law”), and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. As Christian reports , Michigan and especially Texas have both been on the front lines of rising Islamophobia. Michigan has a large Muslim population in cities like Dearborn and Hamtramck, and El-Sayed has drawn particular vitriol; Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) wrote last month that “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic.” And in Texas, as the New York Times reported at length last month , Islamophobia has become a matter of policy as well as rhetoric from Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and other politicians in the state. El-Sayed, in Michigan, has described the attacks as an attempt to distract voters from other issues. “They’re going to point at me, they’re going to point at my name, like, ‘Wow, he’s different,’” he said last month . “My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.” Without much else to run on , though, Republicans seem to have decided they’re all-in on Islamophobia. ➨ Name that song. On Vox’s Unexplainable podcast, the Switched on Pop team looks at how our brains can figure out a song just from its first few seconds, how it can influence our perception, and what we’re losing as recent hits begin to move away from intros. Did you know… that young readers tend to drop off around age 9 , even if they’re prolific readers before that? Publishers aren’t exactly sure why — but they’re hoping a new approach to “middle-grade books” could help reverse some of the decline. Today’s trivia: Which country voted against restarting membership talks with the European Union this year? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in Monday’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the age of the world’s oldest-known oven. That would be 31,000 years old. In 2009, archaeologists discovered an ancient oven in the Czech Republic that dated back to 29,000 BC and was used to roast woolly mammoths, among other things. ##今日，解析通讯：9·11事件25年后，共和党从未如此反穆斯林

##共和党想让美国恐惧穆斯林。作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯，2026年9月11日，UTC晚上10:00

##赠阅 纽约市长佐赫兰·马姆达尼与鲁迪·朱利安尼抵达曼哈顿国家9·11纪念馆和博物馆，出席2026年9月11日举行的25周年纪念仪式。迈克尔·纳格尔/彭博社 via Getty Images

##卡梅伦·彼得斯是Vox的特约编辑。本文发表于《今日，解析》，一份帮助您理解当日最引人注目的新闻和故事的每日通讯。点此订阅。

##各位读者好——今天是9·11事件25周年。在纽约市、华盛顿和宾夕法尼亚州，幸存者、家属和政界人士正聚集在一起，哀悼和纪念那场袭击。今天，我们想聚焦纽约市这个故事中的一个小片段：前市长鲁迪·朱利安尼针对穆斯林市长佐赫兰·马姆达尼参与纪念仪式一事，发表了一通伊斯兰恐惧症式的长篇攻击。需要说明的是，朱利安尼的这番咆哮本身其实算不上新闻；25年过去了，他与其说是“美国市长”，不如说是唐纳德·特朗普总统那位两次被吊销执照、身败名裂的前律师。（而马姆达尼确实出席了活动，甚至与朱利安尼握了手。）但不幸的是，朱利安尼的言论恰恰代表了共和党政治中一个令人不安的趋势——在9·11事件催生出一种尤为丑陋的伊斯兰恐惧症25年之后，公开、咄咄逼人的伊斯兰恐惧症正在抬头。当时与现在的一个主要区别是什么？2001年，许多政客试图压制这种情绪，而非煽动它。正如北卡罗来纳州立大学助理教学教授、《伊斯兰恐惧症产业》一书作者内森·利恩上个月对我同事克里斯蒂安·帕兹所解释的那样：“伊斯兰恐惧症已经通过了餐桌测试。今天，你可以毫无后果地谈论穆斯林。而且它已经被制度化了，这是针对其他边缘化群体的偏见所未能达到的程度。”

##2026年中期选举为右翼的伊斯兰恐惧症转向提供了一个尤为清晰的展示窗口。周四，在德克萨斯州达拉斯市共和党异常的中期代表大会第二晚也是最后一晚，参议员特德·克鲁兹（共和党-德克萨斯州）对与会者说，“共产主义”和“伊斯兰主义”正在结盟对抗共和党人。“他们有着共同的敌人，”他说。“他们仇恨基督徒。他们仇恨犹太人。他们仇恨资本主义。他们仇恨宪法，他们仇恨美国。”在克鲁兹演讲的另一个时刻，当他提到马姆达尼的名字时，与会者尖叫着“他应该被枪毙”，密歇根州民主党

##段落
密歇根州民主党参议员候选人阿卜杜勒·埃尔-赛义德（穆斯林，克鲁兹称其“声称自己有义务遵守伊斯兰教法”），以及得克萨斯州民主党参议员候选人詹姆斯·塔拉里科。正如克里斯蒂安所报道的，密歇根州尤其是得克萨斯州都处于日益高涨的伊斯兰恐惧症的前线。密歇根州在迪尔伯恩和哈姆特拉米克等城市拥有大量穆斯林人口，埃尔-赛义德尤其遭受了恶毒攻击；南卡罗来纳州共和党众议员南希·梅斯上月写道：“在美国担任公职的每一个穆斯林都是一匹特洛伊木马，是对国家安全和我们共和国的威胁。”而在得克萨斯州，正如《纽约时报》上月长篇报道的那样，伊斯兰恐惧症已成为共和党州长格雷格·阿博特及其他该州政客的政策议题，而不仅仅是言辞。密歇根州的埃尔-赛义德将这些攻击描述为试图分散选民对其他问题的注意力。“他们会指着我，会指着我的名字，好像在说，‘哇，他不一样，’”他上个月说。“我的名字没有抬高你的油价。我的名字没有把我们拖入战争。我的名字不是你买不起杂货的原因。”然而，在缺乏其他竞选筹码的情况下，共和党人似乎已决定全力押注伊斯兰恐惧症。

readings.title: The lost species that live on in Irish place names
body: 20 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Chris Baraniuk Irish place names hark back to a world alive with cranes, wolves and eagles. Now these old names are piquing the interest of nature-lovers and ecologists. Along the island of Ireland's southwestern reaches lie craggy headlands blasted by Atlantic storms. This is the very edge of Europe, where County Kerry's breath-taking Dingle peninsula – a crooked finger of black rock and green grass – points resolutely west. And right at the end of that peninsula stands an ocean-facing mountain called Sliabh an Iolair : "Mount Eagle". "That mountain," recalled the famed Irish folk-teller and author Peig Sayers during the early 20th Century, "was full of eagles in my young days, though there isn't one of them left now." An eagle's nest could once be seen on a lakeside cliff atop the mountain, she said. Sayers was born in 1873 and died in 1958. During her lifetime, both mountain-loving golden eagles (iolar fíréan) and white-tailed eagles (iolar mara) went extinct in Ireland . "It is a long time now," the illiterate Sayers told her son in recollections about Sliabh an Iolair that he wrote down , "since there was an eagle's nest there." Ireland is swathed from top to bottom in wonderful Irish place names. Many are richly descriptive, referring to animals, plants, the shape of the land, agricultural practices, and also the weather and climate. There is now growing interest in Ireland, among some, in investigating the meanings of those place names . Researchers are using this information to understand Ireland's ecological past and potentially also to protect its future – by providing precious clues about hidden environmental features. These range from forgotten flood plains to ancient wildlife habitats. "Place names […] are local knowledge – they have emerged over centuries," says Mairéad Nic Craith, a folklorist at the Institute for Northern Studies, part of the University of the Highlands and Islands in Scotland. Irish, one of Europe's oldest living languages, has been spoken in Ireland for more than 2,000 years – and partly as a result of that, its place names capture a long history of people living with the land. However, many of these names were changed or rewritten during English colonisation and the English versions of some place names often lose all or much of the original meaning. Take Tuaim na Mac Tíre , meaning, "grave of the wolf". Wolves became extinct in Ireland during the 18th Century due to hunting and habitat loss, but the old place name reminds us of their historical presence. The English version, "Toom", lacks any reference to wolves. Mac tíre, by the way, means "son of the land", a highly poetic way of referring to a wolf. Wolves come up in many other place names around Ireland, including in some English translations, such as Wolfhill – or, in Irish: Cnocán na Mac Tíre . "There's a connection between the environment and the Irish language," says Nic Craith. "It reflects a people who took more notice, and who had maybe more time to notice the environment than we do nowadays." Last year, Nic Craith and a colleague published a paper arguing that Irish place names are a form of traditional ecological knowledge , since they capture ecological diversity and change. Nic Craith also gives the example of wild boar. The history of boars in Ireland is somewhat murky. Some sources say native boars went extinct in prehistoric times , though others suggest that boar populations, perhaps reintroduced animals, were present well into the medieval era . But anywhere you find turk  (Irish for "boar") in a place name could indicate that location was once home to these animals. Cluain Torc , or Clonturk, means boar's meadow, for example. There's also the crane ( corr ), which comes up in various locations including Oileán na gCorr , or crane island, in County Leitrim. These gangly birds went extinct in Ireland hundreds of years ago . Ecological memory in place names is far from exclusive to animals. Any place called Derry (or, in Irish: doire ) that is now a town or city was quite likely once a wood – doire means wood and often an oak wood, specifically. For thousands of years, Ireland faced successive waves of deforestation, as trees were cleared for farmland and also to extract timber for construction. Various groups, right back to Neolithic and Iron Age Irish peoples, as well as Vikings, Normans and English settlers , took sizeable bites out of Ireland's forests – a history that can be reconstructed by analysing traces of tree pollen preserved in the ground . Eventually, the island was left one of the most deforested places in Europe . As if gesturing back to a leafier past, tree species come up countless times in Irish place names. Take dair, which means oak. It appears in Cill Dara , or Kildare, meaning "church of the oak". There is also Doire na Fuinse , or "ash tree wood". As in many places, ash in Ireland is susceptible to a disease called ash dieback, and most of the remaining trees are expected to disappear . Some Irish place names may not only be a shadow of things lost. They could also point towards a future in which restoration of the environment, or rewilding, brings back certain species or habitats. Just north of Dublin lies a place historically known as Loch Gabhar, which in Old Irish meant lake of (the white) horses. Historically, the Irish word gabhar has been used to mean white horse or goat; today, it means goat. Although there is no lake in this location now, analysis of the subsoil suggests there used to be a larger and a smaller lake there. Researchers recently proposed that these areas might be rewetted to capture floodwater, allowing it to drain into a nearby river. As the risk of flooding grows in Ireland due to climate change, that could in principle make this a place-name-informed climate adaptation. Outside of Ireland, ancient place names are also drawing attention for their ecological potential. Researchers have looked to Old English place names in Britain in the hope of gaining a better understanding of locations at risk of flooding. That could in turn prompt solutions around flood resilience planning. Rewilding projects in Scotland have taken note of Scots Gaelic place names mentioning trees , citing them as potential cues for where tree-planting efforts could occur. But one shouldn't take place names too literally. "Just because a place name mentions a tree or an animal doesn't necessarily mean that that tree or animal was actually there – it might have been a metaphor, it might have been a symbol," says Nic Craith. There is a place I sometimes go sea swimming, not far from Belfast, called Portmuck. It sounds a little off-putting in English, but muc in Irish means pig and some say this was most likely a port that people brought pigs to. Having said that, the nearby Isle of Muck (Oileán na Muc), now a bird sanctuary , looks to me a bit like a pig lying on its front with part of its body submerged. Is that the reason for the name? There's another Isle of Muck in Scotland , in that case apparently named after muc-mara, sea-pigs or whales. Sometimes "muck" has nothing to do with (land-roaming) pigs at all. More like this: •  The true story of Germany's rampant raccoons •  The shark that lives for 400 years •  The wildlife pioneer that inspired Attenborough Ray Ó Foghlú, head of partnerships and development at Hometree, a nature restoration charity in Ireland, says place names are not "instructions" to recreate the past: "Their real value is in showing us what a landscape has been capable of." Ecologists can then test locations for their rewilding potential. Equally, somewhere with no hint of trees or woods in its name could actually be a perfect site, today, for a tree-planting project, for example. Nic Craith describes place names as "a starting point". And who knows where they will lead you. Although Peig Sayers never lived to see it, white-tailed eagles were reintroduced to County Kerry in 2007 , at Killarney National Park, roughly 52 miles (83km) from Sliabh an Iolair. There are now roughly 150 white-tailed eagles in the wild in Ireland. They are breeding, and sustaining their own population. Golden eagle reintroductions are also underway elsewhere on the island. Tantalisingly, some of the white-tailed eagles have even found their way back to the area around Sliabh an Iolair . Perhaps eagles will one day build a new nest on that famous mountain. A place that, once again, is named after animals living in this part of the world – memories reborn. -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . ##段落
20小时前 分享 保存 在Google上添加为首选 Chris Baraniuk 爱尔兰的地名让人回想起一个鹤、狼和鹰活跃其间的世界。如今这些古老的名字引起了自然爱好者和生态学家的兴趣。爱尔兰岛西南端延伸着被大西洋风暴肆虐的崎岖海岬。这里是欧洲的最边缘，凯里郡令人叹为观止的丁格尔半岛——一根由黑色岩石和绿草组成的弯曲手指——坚定地指向西方。而就在半岛的尽头，矗立着一座面朝大海的山，名为Sliabh an Iolair：“鹰山”。20世纪初，爱尔兰著名民间故事讲述者和作家佩格·赛尔斯回忆道：“在我年轻时，那座山上到处都是鹰，尽管现在一只都不剩了。”她说，曾经可以在山顶湖畔的悬崖上看到鹰巢。赛尔斯生于1873年，卒于1958年。在她的一生中，热爱山地的金雕（iolar fíréan）和白尾海雕（iolar mara）都在爱尔兰灭绝了。不识字의 赛尔斯在向儿子口述关于Sliabh an Iolair的回忆时说道——由他儿子记录下来——“已经过去很久了，那里曾经有一个鹰巢。”

##段落
爱尔兰从上到下遍布着美妙的爱尔兰地名。许多地名描述性极强，涉及动物、植物、地形地貌、农业实践以及天气和气候。如今在爱尔兰，一些人对于探究这些地名的含义兴趣日益浓厚。研究人员正在利用这些信息来了解爱尔兰的生态历史，并有可能借此保护其未来——通过提供关于隐藏环境特征的珍贵线索。这些线索涵盖从被遗忘的洪泛平原到古代野生动物栖息地等各种内容。“地名……是本地知识——它们是经过数百年逐渐形成的，”苏格兰高地与群岛大学北方研究所的民俗学家梅雷德·尼克·克莱斯说道。爱尔兰语是欧洲现存最古老的语言之一，在爱尔兰已使用了2000多年——部分正因如此，其地名记录了人与土地共处的悠久历史。然而，许多地名在英国殖民时期被更改或重写，一些地名的英文版本往往完全丧失了原意或丢失了大部分含义。以Tuaim na Mac Tíre为例，意为“狼之墓”。由于猎杀和栖息地丧失，狼在18世纪的爱尔兰灭绝了，但这个古老的地名提醒着我们它们曾经的存在。其英文版本“Toom”则完全不提狼。顺便说一句，Mac tíre意为“大地之子”，是对狼一种极具诗意의 称呼。狼还出现在爱尔兰许多其他地名中，包括

##段落
在一些英文翻译中也有体现，例如Wolfhill——或者用爱尔兰语说：Cnocán na Mac Tíre。“环境与爱尔兰语之间存在一种联系，”Nic Craith说。“它反映了一个比我们如今更留意、也许有更多时间去留意环境的民族。”去年，Nic Craith和一位同事发表了一篇论文，认为爱尔兰地名是一种传统生态知识的形式，因为它们记录了生态多样性与变化。Nic Craith还举了野猪的例子。野猪在爱尔兰的历史有些模糊。一些资料称本土野猪在史前时期就已灭绝，但也有人指出，野猪种群——可能是被重新引入的动物——一直存续到中世纪时期。但无论你在哪里发现地名中含有turk（爱尔兰语意为“野猪”），都可能表明该地曾是这些动物的家园。例如，Cluain Torc，即Clonturk，意为野猪的草地。还有鹤（corr），它出现在多个地名中，包括利特里姆郡的Oileán na gCorr，即鹤岛。这些瘦长的鸟类数百年前已在爱尔兰灭绝。地名中的生态记忆远不限于动物。任何现在已是城镇、名为Derry（爱尔兰语：doire）的地方，很可能曾经是一片树林——doire意为树林，且通常特指橡树林。数千年来，爱尔兰经历了接连不断的毁林浪潮，树木被砍伐以开辟农田，也用于获取建筑木材。从新石器时代和铁器时代的爱尔兰人，到维京人、诺曼人和英格兰定居者，各个群体都对爱尔兰的森林大肆蚕食——这段历史可以通过分析保存在地下的树木花粉痕迹来重建。最终，这座岛成为欧洲森林砍伐最严重的地方之一。仿佛在回望一个枝叶更繁茂的过去，树种在爱尔兰地名中出现了无数次。以dair为例，意为橡树。它出现在Cill Dara，即基尔代尔，意为“橡树教堂”。还有Doire na Fuinse，意为“白蜡树林”。与许多地方一样，爱尔兰的白蜡树易患一种名为白蜡树枯萎病的疾病，预计剩余的大部分树木将会消失。一些爱尔兰地名可能不仅仅是失落之物的影子。它们还可能指向一个未来——在那个未来里，环境修复或再野化让某些物种或栖息地得以回归。都柏林正北方有一个历史上称为Loch Gabhar的地方，在古爱尔兰语中意为（白）马之湖。历史上，爱尔兰语词汇gabhar曾被用来表示白马或山羊；如今，它的意思是山羊。尽管该地现在没有湖泊，但对底土的分析表明，这里曾经有一个较大的和一个较小的

## 那里的湖。研究人员最近提出，这些地区可以重新湿润以蓄积洪水，让洪水排入附近的河流。随着气候变化导致爱尔兰洪水风险加剧，这原则上可以成为一种以地名为依据的气候适应措施。在爱尔兰以外，古老地名也因其生态潜力而受到关注。研究人员研究了英国的古英语地名，希望更好地了解面临洪水风险的地点。这反过来可以推动洪水韧性规划方面的解决方案。苏格兰的再野化项目注意到了提及树木的苏格兰盖尔语地名，将其视为可能适合植树地点的线索。但人们不应过于字面地理解地名。“仅仅因为一个地名提到了某种树或某种动物，并不一定意味着那种树或那种动物真的曾在那里——它可能是一个隐喻，也可能是一个象征，”尼克·克莱斯说道。有一个我有时去海泳的地方，离贝尔法斯特不远，叫波特马克。它在英语里听起来有点令人反感，但爱尔兰语中的muc意思是猪，有人说这很可能是一个人们把猪运到的港口。话虽如此，附近的马克岛（Oileán na Muc），如今是一个鸟类保护区，在我看来有点像一头趴着的猪，部分身体浸在水中。这就是这个名字的由来吗？苏格兰还有另一个马克岛，在那个例子中，显然是得名于muc-mara，即海猪或鲸鱼。有时候“muck”和（陆地上活动的）猪毫无关系。更多类似内容：• 德国浣熊泛滥的真实故事 • 活了400年的鲨鱼 • 启发阿滕伯勒的野生动物先驱雷·奥福格鲁是爱尔兰自然修复慈善机构Hometree的合作伙伴关系与发展负责人，他说地名并不是重现过去的“指令”：“它们真正的价值在于向我们展示一片土地曾经能够承载什么。”生态学家随后可以测试各地点的再野化潜力。同样，某个地名中完全没有树木或森林痕迹的地方，如今实际上可能是一个植树项目的完美选址。尼克·克莱斯将地名描述为“一个起点”。谁知道它们会把你引向何方。尽管佩格·塞耶斯生前未能看到，白尾海雕于2007年被重新引入凯里郡的基拉尼国家公园，距离Sliabh an Iolair约52英里（83公里）。目前爱尔兰野外大约有150只白尾海雕。它们正在繁殖，并维持着自己的种群。该岛其他地方也在进行金雕的重新引入。令人遐想的是，一些白尾海雕甚至已经回到了Sliab

## 在“鹰巢”之地，也许有一天，鹰会在这座著名的山上筑起新的巢穴。一个再次以生活在这片土地上的动物命名的地方——重生的记忆。

readings.title: How social media ceased to be social
body: 22 May 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Social media platforms used to be about communication between friends – now many are increasingly short video entertainment hubs. The business model is to increase the time people spend on their apps and increase ad revenue. But is there already a consumer backlash? Aurélia fixes herself a coffee, sits down in her beautiful garden not far from Paris and goes on Instagram "to relax." First up: "a guy I like a lot who does interior design. He's in Venice at the moment." She's into interior design, and has even just had two bird drawings by the 19th Century English designer William Morris tattooed on her arms. She scrolls down. Two kittens having a fight. "I love animals so I get a lot of animals. That's how it works, social media. You click on bananas and they give you bananas." There are ads too – although they look just like the other posts – for a robot-vacuum cleaner, a diet and bed linen (with Morris-inspired designs). But no friends. She has 198 on Instagram but she says "it's completely changed. I practically don’t see any friends' posts anymore." She’s pretty much given up posting herself. "I don't think anyone sees them anymore anyway."  While there remain committed social, amateur posters on Instagram and especially Facebook, the switch from communicating with people you know to scrolling through professionally made content from people you don't, is even more pronounced among young users. Kylian, 16, is in vocational training to become a chef. He's on TikTok and Youtube a lot, he says. "I like looking at videos more than photos or messages. I watch videos made by people I don't know. I don’t post at all. I'm a rather shy person. I stay in my bubble. I watch and that’s all. I keep my reactions to myself." "I spend a lot of time scrolling through videos made by content-creators," says Lucie, also 16. "They're more interesting than the posts of people I know." She doesn't post except sometimes "stories" which disappear after 24 hours.  Whether it's TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram, we are a long way from the "digital town square" of personal interaction that social media was even just a few years ago. In France, annual official Barometre du numerique 2026  shows 49% of social media users are "active only occasionally". In the UK, an Ofcom report   published in April showed a year-on-year drop of users who actively post from 61% to 49%. In the US, a Morning Consult survey of June last year found 28% reported posting less often than the previous year. Just 33% now post daily compared to 57% who use it for entertainment daily. The gap is a lot wider still for Gen Z – 18% active for 74% passive. Vanessa Lalo, a Paris-based clinical psychologist specialising in on-line behaviour, says "users have become more conscious that the traces you leave (on social media) stay there forever and some no longer want to maintain social media relations that can be superficial. Some don’t want the exposure to criticism that might be a risk when you post or the feeling that their post will seem poor alongside all the professional content". However, Lalo adds, people haven’t stopped posting, rather they are posting different things and in different places. "On TikTok, for example, young people publish a lot of content but it's more funny parodies and remixes of existing material. The goal is to make people laugh, not to tell people about their lives." That still happens, she says, but it’s moved from social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook to messaging sites like WhatsApp. There's also been a move towards private groups on Instagram and Snapchat. "These are much more intimate places where you're not bombarded with ads and content made by influencers," she says. "What we're seeing is social media splitting in two," says social media consultant Matt Navarra, author of the Geekout Newsletter. "Big platforms like Instagram and TikTok are becoming more about entertainment and discovery. WhatsApp is becoming the place people go to actually be social. The catch is, those kinds of spaces are harder for companies to make money from." Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business – Matt Navarra It was TikTok that helped to pioneer an algorithm that figures out from the moment you start scrolling what you like, and then fills your feed with material calculated to keep you on the app for the longest possible time. Now, says Matt Navarra, "Meta has built what it calls an AI system for unconnected content recommendations on Facebook and Instagram, which basically means, they're increasingly showing you stuff from people you don't follow because the machine thinks you're going to like it. It's not biased towards, is it a professional creator? Is it a brand? Is it a friend? If they can see that you've engaged with a friend a lot, you might see a lot more of their content. It's just that who you are friends with, who you follow, has become irrelevant in a way." This all means that small businesses, that have long used social media for free promotion have to up their game.   "There's a real opportunity for some small businesses," says Matt Navarra. "A bakery, florist, salon or local café can still break through if they have a good story, strong visuals or behind-the-scenes content people want to watch. But it also means the job has changed. Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business." The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow – Matt Navarra Social media is evolving into something passive like television, albeit television that adapts as you zap. Or rather which knows you so well that it doesn't seem to matter that much that it's taken the remote control. You give the platform information about yourself that it uses for commercial gain and, in return, it gives you content tailored to please you for free. The transition from truly social media to entertainment platform does seem to be paying off. "The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow," says Matt Navarra. Global social media ad revenue is expected to reach $317 billion (£236bn) in 2026, up from $277 billion (£206bn) last year. Meta is the biggest winner. Its ad sales already increased 22% year-on-year in 2025.  Ad sales are expected to hit $243 billion (£181bn) this year , enough to overtake Google for the first time. AI powered digital ad targeting is becoming ever more effective and precise. "The social platforms allow companies to put ads amongst the content that you're scrolling through. Every third or fourth scroll is an ad. And they are the world's best ad targeting engines. They know so much about your interests because of what you've looked at, liked, engaged with, what you've chosen to follow, the time you've spent in certain areas of the app, things like that," Navarra says.  "So advertisers will go in and say: 'I want to place an ad next to people in the UK who are between thirty and sixty years old and who are interested in DIY' and the social platforms will have that information and will place the ads accordingly." The price will depend on the number of impressions (clicks) the advertiser wants and how tight the criteria are. It costs more to place ads in the social media feeds of people who buy horses than people who buy ice-cream. More like this: •  TikTok is tracking you, even if you don't use the app. Here's how to stop it •  How to stop AI from turning your brain to mush •  This monkey selfie will protect you from AI slop Might there be a backlash coming? Don't many people go on to social media to see how friends are reacting to their posts or comments before settling down to scroll through professionally made content? Whether it's the shrinking social motivation to get on these apps or something else, the amount of time people spend on social media plateaued at an average of 141 minutes in 2025, down slightly from 143 minutes in 2024 . However, this is only part of the story, as the number of people using social media and the total time humanity spends on these apps continues to rise. For Gen Z it’s higher still. Around five hours a day in the United States where, for this demographic, social media has also become the primary search engine and shopping tool. Meanwhile, for those who miss what are fast becoming the old days when social media enabled you to share a bit of your life, a joke or a point of view with people you more-or-less knew, there are tools within platforms, says Matt Navarra, that allow you to choose to see mainly friends and family content. "People can flick to a feed that gives them that," he says. "But most people don't." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.   For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 2026年5月22日 分享 收藏 在Google上添加为首选 约翰·劳伦森 社交媒体平台曾经是关于朋友之间交流的——如今许多平台正日益变成短视频娱乐中心。其商业模式是增加人们在应用上花费的时间，并提高广告收入。但消费者是否已经出现了反弹？奥蕾莉亚给自己冲了杯咖啡，坐在巴黎附近她美丽的花园里，打开Instagram“放松一下”。首先出现的是：“一个我很喜欢的做室内设计的人。他现在在威尼斯。”她喜欢室内设计，甚至刚在手臂上纹了两幅19世纪英国设计师威廉·莫里斯的鸟类画作。她往下滑动。两只小猫在打架。“我喜欢动物，所以我看到很多动物。社交媒体就是这样运作的。你点击香蕉，它就给你香蕉。”还有广告——尽管它们看起来和其他帖子一模一样——推销机器人吸尘器、减肥方案和床品（带有莫里斯风格的设计）。但没有朋友。她在Instagram上有198个好友，但她说“情况完全变了。我几乎再也看不到朋友的帖子了。”她基本上已经放弃自己发帖了。“反正我觉得也没人看得到了。”虽然Instagram、尤其是Facebook上仍有忠实的社交型业余发帖者，但从与认识的人交流转向浏览不认识的人制作的专业内容，这一转变在年轻用户中更为明显。16岁的基利安正在接受职业培训，准备成为厨师。他说自己大量使用TikTok和YouTube。“比起照片或消息，我更喜欢看视频。我看不认识的人做的视频。我完全不发帖。我是个相当害羞的人。我待在自己的泡泡里。我只看，仅此而已。我把自己的反应留在心里。”同样16岁的露西说：“我花很多时间刷内容创作者做的视频。它们比我认识的人发的帖子更有意思。”她不发帖，只是有时发“快拍”，24小时后就会消失。无论是TikTok、Snapchat、Facebook还是Instagram，我们都已远离社交媒体仅仅几年前还是个人互动的“数字城市广场”的时代。在法国，年度官方《2026数字晴雨表》显示，49%的社交媒体用户“只是偶尔活跃”。在英国，Ofcom于4月发布的一份报告显示，活跃发帖用户同比从61%降至49%。在美国，Morning Consult去年6月的一项调查发现，28%的人表示发帖频率低于前一年。如今只有33%的人每天发帖，而57%的人每天将社交媒体用于娱乐。对于Z世代，这一差距还要大得多——18%活跃，74%被动。凡妮莎·拉洛，巴黎临床心理学家，专攻网络行为

社交媒体正在演变成一种类似电视的被动媒介，只不过是一台会随着你换台而自适应调整的电视。或者说，它太了解你了，以至于它夺走了遥控器这件事似乎也没那么重要。你向平台提供关于自己的信息，平台将其用于商业获利，作为回报，它免费为你提供量身定制、取悦你的内容。从真正的社交媒体向娱乐平台的转变，似乎确实带来了回报。“社交平台的主要变现方式仍然是广告收入。这依然是核心商业模式。而且广告收入仍在持续增长，”马特·纳瓦拉说道。全球社交媒体广告收入预计将在2026年达到3170亿美元（2360亿英镑），高于去年的2770亿美元（2060亿英镑）。Meta是最大的赢家。其广告销售额在2025年已经同比增长22%。今年广告销售额预计将达到2430亿美元（1810亿英镑），足以首次超越谷歌。人工智能驱动的数字广告定向投放正变得越来越高效和精准。“社交平台允许企业将广告植入你正在浏览的内容之中。每刷三四条就有一条是广告。而且它们是世界上最好的广告定向引擎。它们对你的兴趣了如指掌，因为知道你看了什么、点赞了什么、参与了什么、选择关注了谁、在应用某些板块停留了多长时间，诸如此类，”纳瓦拉说。“所以广告主会进去说：‘我想把广告投给英国30到60岁、对DIY感兴趣的人’，社交平台掌握这些信息，就会相应地投放广告。”价格取决于广告主想要的曝光量（点击量）以及定向条件的严格程度。把广告投放到买马的人的社交媒体信息流中，比投给买冰淇淋的人要贵。

readings.title: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do
body: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do

Ever have your hard work — including your successes — go unnoticed by your manager? Fixable , TED’s new podcast, is here to do just that — to fix the problems of everyday people who call in with their work woes.

In episode four , cohosts and top leadership coaches Frances Frei and Anne Morriss got to know Nai’a, a caller who struggled with receiving recognition after a major reorganization paired her with a new and preoccupied boss. Nai’a was going above and beyond to do her job well, but the lack of acknowledgement and encouragement — and even awareness — of her work was causing her to lose motivation.
Frances’s and Anne’s first piece of advice to Nai’a was simple: See the humanness of what’s going on — and of your manager.

“Sometimes the barrier to showing up as a great collaborator with your manager can be that there’s still some residual frustration about the situation,” Anne explained. “But that emotion is not going to be useful to you.”
Instead, they encouraged Nai’a to recognize the humanity of her manager and forgive them for making mistakes.
Frances and Anne also shared this strategy with her to practice: Choose curiosity over judgment.

Here’s how Frances put it: “You have a choice between judgment and curiosity, because both can’t exist at the same time. So if you have judgment about your manager, you can’t really be curious about their situation. And when you’re thinking of your manager as a person who’s got a lot of part-time jobs, how do we set them up for success?”

“The simplest expression of curiosity — which is truly a magical elixir in a workplace — is in the form of questions,” said Anne. For example, you could start by asking your manager what process works best for them to learn about your accomplishments and contributions. Or, you could focus on how you can make your meetings with them more productive by asking them, “How can our one-on-one time be of service to what we’re trying to achieve together?”

Another option: Be open about your concerns, and ask your manager what their vision of your success looks like. You could say something like, “Here’s my fear: I’m working really hard, and in this state of flux, I’m afraid that six months will go by and people are going to wonder whether or not I did a good job. So it’s just helpful for me to be clear — what is a good job and how can I help in getting that data for you?”

Across industries and across the world, many people are going through workplace reorganizations and other sweeping changes. And like Nai’a, it’s normal to feel anxious and stressed by what’s happening and to need to go through a readjustment period. Leading with questions — and seeing your boss as another human you’re collaborating with — can help you gain back some agency and autonomy.

“Try doing what you can, and marvel at how the other person changes as a result, as opposed to coming up with the list of how you would like the other person to change,” said Frances. “I think you’re going to be pleasantly surprised; that’s the beautiful part of this.”

No matter your job or business, you’ll find actionable advice on Fixable that can improve your workdays. In other episodes, learn how to overcome communication roadblocks, scale up your side project and lead more productive meetings. ##段落
你是否曾经历过自己的辛勤付出——包括那些亮眼的成绩——却被上司视而不见？TED的新播客节目《Fixable》正是为此而生——帮那些来电倾诉职场烦恼的普通人解决实际问题。

##段落
在第四期节目中，联合主持人、顶尖领导力教练弗朗西斯·弗雷和安妮·莫里斯认识了一位来电者奈阿。在一次大规模组织架构调整后，奈阿被分配了一位新的、精力分散的上司，她因此难以获得应有的认可。奈阿一直在竭尽全力把工作做好，但缺乏认可和鼓励——甚至上司对她的工作毫不知情——让她逐渐失去了动力。

##段落
弗朗西斯和安妮给奈阿的第一条建议很简单：看到事情本身的人性面——也看到你上司的人性面。

##段落
“有时候，阻碍你与上司建立良好协作关系的，可能是你对现状仍心存不满，”安妮解释道，“但这种情绪对你没有任何帮助。”

##段落
相反，她们鼓励奈阿去理解上司作为普通人的一面，并原谅他们也会犯错。

##段落
弗朗西斯和安妮还分享了一个可以练习的策略：选择好奇，而非评判。

##段落
弗朗西斯是这样说的：“你可以在评判和好奇之间做选择，因为两者无法同时存在。如果你对上司抱有评判，你就无法真正对他们的处境感到好奇。当你把上司看作一个身兼多职的人时，我们要怎样帮助他们走向成功？”

##段落
“好奇最简单的表达方式——它堪称职场中的神奇灵药——就是以提问的形式呈现，”安妮说。比如，你可以先问上司，什么样的方式最便于他们了解你的成绩和贡献。或者，你可以聚焦于如何让你们之间的会议更高效，问他们：“我们的一对一时间怎样才能更好地服务于我们共同想达成的目标？”

##段落
另一个选择：坦诚地说出你的担忧，问上司他们眼中你的成功是什么样的。你可以这样说：“我的担忧是这样的：我非常努力地工作，但在这种变动的状态下，我怕半年过去后，大家会质疑我到底有没有做好。所以对我来说，把话说清楚会很有帮助——什么算做得好，以及我怎样才能帮你获取这些信息？”

##段落
在各行各业、世界各地，许多人都正在经历职场重组和其他大规模变革。和奈阿一样，对正在发生的变化感到焦虑和压力、需要一段重新适应的时期，都是再正常不过的。

带着问题去沟通——把老板也看作与你协作的普通人——能帮你找回一些主动权和自主性。
“试着做你能做的事，然后惊叹于对方因此发生的变化，而不是列出一张你希望对方如何改变的清单，”弗朗西斯说。“我想你会惊喜地发现；这正是这件事美妙的地方。”
无论你从事什么工作或业务，你都能在《Fixable》中找到可操作的建议，改善你的工作日。在其他剧集中，你还能学习如何克服沟通障碍、扩大你的副业规模，以及主持更高效的会议。另外：点击这里，有机会在节目中让你的工作问题得到解答！现在就可在你收听播客的任何平台收听《Fixable》。

readings.title: The GOP midterms strategy is Trump and a prayer
body: America, Actually The GOP midterms strategy is Trump and a prayer What we learned from the first day of the Republican convention in Dallas. by Astead Herndon Sep 10, 2026, 10:40 PM UTC Gift People hold signs on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Astead Herndon is a host and editorial director at Vox, helping lead politics coverage across text, video, audio, and social media platforms. Welcome to The Midterms, Actually. Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every week. Let’s get into it. The first-of-its-kind Republican midterms convention began in the same vein as President Donald Trump’s second term: open grift. The president announced a pledge to give every American $5,000 if Republicans win the House and the Senate — part of what he’s calling a new dividend for American voters, and what some Democrats are calling an attempted bribe. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Obviously, there are lots of questions about Trump’s announcement: Who will pay for the $1 trillion-plus dividend? Taxpayers. Could this even happen without congressional approval? Probably not . Why not just vote on it now, while Republicans control Congress? It would likely fail . But I think the pronouncement — and the GOP convention broadly — is best understood as a proxy for the Republican message in the midterm elections, not a policy roadmap for what Trump would do if Republicans maintained control of the House and Senate. So what can we actually glean from the GOP’s two-day bonanza in Dallas, and how does the message they were offering on that made-for-TV platform match up with the message they’ve delivered on the campaign trail? I took a close look at the convention speeches on Wednesday and Thursday, dug through our America, Actually reporting focusing on Republican voters and their candidates, and pulled together some trends that help explain the GOP strategy for defying the odds (and the polling) come Election Day. 1. Republicans are mostly in hiding — One reason Trump’s midterm convention sticks out in this year’s landscape: It’s one of the rare places Republicans will campaign out loud. Congressional candidates, even in battleground House districts, have rarely held public events or town halls this year. And as Trump’s unpopularity has continued to grow, driven by rising gas prices and an unpopular war with Iran, it’s not like the GOP has responded by mounting a defense of its leader. They’ve mostly gone AWOL, a result of the electoral pickle the president has put them in. Trump is undoubtedly still the most powerful figure within the party, particularly among the Republican base, but Trump is also the biggest motivator for the Democratic base, and is increasingly off-putting to independent voters, who backed him in 2024. His approval has sunk to 33 percent in one recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest of his presidency , and that same poll found Democrats markedly more fired up for the midterms than Republicans — an enthusiasm gap that’s poison for the party in power. The independents who put him over the top have soured as the war drags on: a UMass poll found more than two-thirds disapprove of his handling of Iran nationally, and four in five say the war has driven up their gas and food prices. So when Trump tells voters at the GOP midterm convention to “pretend that he’s on the ballot” and turn out in November, I think his opponents listen with glee. Democrats are in the position they’re in because of a brewing electoral backlash to Trump — and the reason Republicans are so hard to find on the campaign trail is that they sense that same backlash is brewing, too. Check out what Ted Cruz said on The View this week: “The big open question is, do Republicans show up?” Cruz asked. “If we stay home, there’s a blue wave.” 2. Even Trump is on the defensive — It’s rare to see Trump acknowledge any semblance of failure, but he came close during his speech during the convention’s first night. Trump was clearly on the defensive throughout his remarks: he sought to make the case for his (unpopular) tariff policy, he defended the (deeply unpopular) Iran war but without the usual bluster, and he acknowledged that gas prices may not fall until after Election Day. Last year, he predicted gas prices would soon hit $2 a gallon; this week he’s asking for still more patience after they hit a record $4.15 on Labor Day . From his speech: “You know, it happens to me all the time. Guys come up, ‘You know, I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran, gasoline’s up, ba, ba, ba.’ And I say, ‘Well, let me ask you…let me ask you one question. Can Iran have a nuclear weapon?’ ‘Absolutely not.’ ‘Well, then I’m right, then I win, okay?’” But it’s worth remembering that “be patient” is a controversial message even among Republican voters. When our America, Actually team spent a day outside gas stations in Allentown this summer — deep in PA-7, one of the most contested House districts in the country ( watch the episode ) — we heard a clean split. There were some Republicans willing to eat the higher price in service of Trump’s war: “Yes, because our president is actually doing something about Iran. He’s not sugarcoating it. It’s something we need to do, and in the long run it’s gonna be better for everybody.” And there were other Republicans who voted for Trump and are furious: “I voted for him with his promises to the American people…and I think he’s let us down.” Another put the broken promise plainly: “I blame the president because he indicated to us he’s gonna drop all these costs. I know it can’t happen overnight, but when is it gonna happen? It’s outrageous.” The message now is to wait until after the election. A lot of the president’s own voters at the pump aren’t sure they can. 3. Notice the candidates who weren’t there — Maybe the most revealing thing about Trump’s convention was the guest list, or more notably, the no-shows. MAGA celebrities who owe their careers to Trump packed the stage, but not a lot of the Republicans who are actually on the ballot in places they must win. Notable absences include candidates like John Sununu in New Hampshire and Susan Collins in Maine, and various congressional candidates from battleground races. And while their political calculus may be obvious — they want to avoid a Dallas-with-Trump photo op that ends up in a challenger’s attack ad — it reflects the “win by hiding” strategy that candidates not named Vivek Ramaswamy seem to be deploying. Here’s the play in a nutshell: keep enough distance from Trump to maintain credibility and independence, but rely on Trump to raise money, drive up Republican turnout, and savagely attack Democratic opponents. When conservative activist CJ Pearson came on our show , he insisted the GOP doesn’t have an electability problem at all — voters will see Democrats as too radical on topics like socialism and transgender women in sports, which came up repeatedly in the convention, and Republicans can still find ways to address affordability concerns. “These are 80/20 issues,” he said. ”And so I actually really like our odds here…we’re going to overperform. The Senate, we’re gonna hold onto. The House will be a dogfight, but I like our chances.” He even predicted this exact week, telling me the party would “see a change in his messaging and a reset at the midterm convention in Dallas,” after which “you’ll see those numbers start to change.” Whether Dallas actually delivered that reset — or just a $5,000 bribe and a defensive Trump — is, generously, an open question. And the attendance sheet suggests some of Pearson’s own party’s candidates aren’t waiting around to find out. 4. The JD Vance tightrope — One person who doesn’t have the benefit of keeping distance from Trump is JD Vance, his vice president and the presumed GOP frontrunner for the 2028 presidential nomination. He’s close to right-wing voices who have soured on Trump, and has to worry about voters longer than the president will have to, and the Iran war, tariffs, and Trump’s promises all present conflicts for him. Just last week, he took heat from prominent voices in Trump’s coalition for his refusal to disavow Tucker Carlson , the podcast host and former TV anchor who’s become a vocal critic of the Israeli government and Trump’s second-term agenda. Looking ahead to his speech tonight, I’ll be watching how carefully he handles Trump’s tariffs, the Iran war, and gas prices. He’s tried to strike a more empathetic note on the economy than Trump, who has described talk of an affordability crisis as a made-up narrative to hurt him politically that — to the extent it was real — was President Joe Biden’s fault anyway. “They caused [it], but we’re fixing it,” the president said Wednesday. Vance says he won’t “sit down” with Trump to discuss his 2028 plans until after the midterms, but Trump is not the kind of person who seems likely to give his successor a lot of room to run away from his record. This week I talked to Charlotte Matherly, a reporter at the Concord Monitor who has been following the underdiscussed New Hampshire Senate race. New Hampshire is one of the Democrats’ must-win states to take back the Senate, but there’s been some concern that Republican candidate John Sununu — a former New Hampshire senator with a long family legacy in the state — could give Democratic nominee Rep. Chris Pappas deep problems. I talked to Matherly about lessons from the state’s primary and what to expect in the general election. So, the New Hampshire primary just happened — what were the takeaways? And why has this race gone under the radar? With the progressive versus moderate conversation happening nationally, that was my biggest question heading into Tuesday. Would we see that progressive wave or ripple or whatever you want to call it here too? Because we did have a progressive candidate [Karishma Manzur] run against Chris Pappas, who really focused on humanitarianism and ending what she saw as US complicity in foreign wars. Voters who liked her were really passionate about her, but in the end, I think people just wanted to vote for what they know, and [Pappas] was already in Congress. The progressive wave that we’ve seen across the country has not necessarily translated here. Why do you think New Hampshire has stood apart from the national progressive wave? To give you context for New Hampshire politics, it’s always kind of different from the national electorate. We’re a true purple state — independents are the largest voting bloc here. But there are some quirks. Like, for the past 20 years, except for a few exceptions, voters tend to send Republicans to the state legislature, but usually vote for Democrats when it comes to Congress or presidential elections. So splitting your ticket is really common here. And I hear from people every time I go out to the polls that someone has switched their party in the past few years, or they fall back and forth. So it’s really hard to tell where the partisan lines fall here. How has the Republican candidate, John Sununu, handled Donald Trump’s popularity? Years ago [in 2024], Sununu actually penned an op-ed calling Donald Trump a “loser.” And there’s been some bite from the party about that. But Trump actually ended up endorsing him, and he’s also shared the backing of powerful fundraisers and a lot of conservative organizations hoping to flip the seat red. But still, Sununu is trying to emphasize his independence from the administration. He’s saying he’s not worried about currying favor or anything like that, but he hasn’t really put too many policy differences between himself and Trump. One example that I can think of is that he said he opposed the [reported $300 billion] included in Trump’s deal with Iran that was earmarked for reconstruction. He had said he didn’t think that the US should provide any money for reconstruction. And so there’s been a few things like that that he has tried to sort of strike out on his own from the president. ##段落
他们已经完全擅离职守，这是总统让他们陷入选举困境的结果。特朗普无疑仍是党内最有权势的人物，尤其是在共和党基础选民中，但特朗普也是民主党基础选民最大的动员力量，并且越来越让独立选民反感，而这些独立选民曾在2024年支持过他。在最近一项路透社/益普索民调中，他的支持率已跌至33%，为其总统任期内最低；同一项民调还发现，民主党人对中期选举的热情明显高于共和党人——这种热情差距对执政党而言是毒药。随着战争持续，那些曾将他推上胜利宝座的独立选民已经转而不满：马萨诸塞大学的一项民调发现，超过三分之二的人不赞成他在全国层面处理伊朗问题的方式，五分之四的人表示这场战争推高了他们的汽油和食品价格。所以，当特朗普在共和党中期选举大会上告诉选民要“假装他也在选票上”，并在11月出来投票时，我认为他的对手是带着窃喜在听的。民主党人之所以处于现在的位置，是因为一场正在酝酿的对特朗普的选举反弹——而共和党人在竞选活动中如此难觅踪影，是因为他们也感觉到同样的反弹正在酝酿。看看特德·克鲁兹本周在《观点》节目上说的话：“最大的未解问题是，共和党人会出来投票吗？”克鲁兹问道。“如果我们待在家里，就会出现蓝色浪潮。”

##段落
2. 连特朗普也处于守势——很少看到特朗普承认任何类似失败的东西，但他在大会第一晚的演讲中已经接近承认了。特朗普在整个讲话中显然处于守势：他试图为自己的（不受欢迎的）关税政策辩护，他为（极不受欢迎的）伊朗战争辩护，但没有往常那种大言不惭，他还承认汽油价格可能要到选举日之后才会下降。去年，他预测汽油价格很快就会降到每加仑2美元；本周，在汽油价格于劳动节达到创纪录的4.15美元后，他却要求人们再耐心一点。他在演讲中说：“你知道，这种事总发生在我身上。有人走上来，‘你知道，我希望你没打伊朗，汽油涨了，叭叭叭。’我说，‘那好，让我问你……让我问你一个问题。伊朗能有核武器吗？’‘绝对不能。’‘那好，那就是我对，那我就赢了，行吧？’”但值得记住的是，“保持耐心”即使在共和党选民中也是有争议的信息。今年夏天，我们的《美国，其实》团队在阿伦敦的加油站外待了一天——深入宾夕法尼亚州第七选区，这是全国竞争最激烈的众议院选区之一（观看那一集）——我们听到的是泾渭分明的分歧。有些共和党人愿意为了特朗普的战争承受更高价格：“是的，因为我们的总统确实在对伊朗采取行动。他没有粉饰。这是我们必须做的事，从长远看它g

##段落
对所有人来说都会更好。”还有其他投票支持特朗普的共和党人如今怒不可遏：“我投票给他，是因为他对美国人民许下的承诺……我觉得他让我们失望了。”另一位则直白地点破了这桩背弃的承诺：“我怪总统，因为他向我们表示他会把这些成本全都降下来。我知道这不可能一夜之间实现，但什么时候才能实现？这太离谱了。”现在传出的信息是：等到选举之后再说。而总统自己的许多选民在加油站前，并不确定自己等不等得起。

##段落
3. 注意那些没到场的人——也许特朗普这场大会最有揭示意义的，是嘉宾名单，或者更准确地说，是缺席者。靠特朗普起家的MAGA名流挤满了舞台，但真正要在必须赢下的选区参选的共和党人却没几个到场。值得注意的缺席者包括新罕布什尔州的约翰·苏努努、缅因州的苏珊·柯林斯，以及来自各摇摆选区的多位国会议员候选人。他们的政治算计或许显而易见——他们想避免一场“达拉斯与特朗普同框”的作秀，最终出现在挑战者的攻击广告里——但这也反映出一种“靠躲藏来取胜”的策略，除了维韦克·拉马斯瓦米之外，候选人似乎都在采用这一策略。这套打法的要点是：与特朗普保持足够距离，以维持可信度和独立性，但又要依赖特朗普来筹款、拉高共和党投票率，并凶狠地攻击民主党对手。当保守派活动人士CJ·皮尔逊做客我们的节目时，他坚称共和党根本不存在 electability（可当选性）问题——选民会认为民主党人在社会主义、跨性别女性参加体育运动等议题上过于激进，这些议题在大会上被反复提及，而共和党人仍能找到办法回应民众对负担能力的担忧。“这些是80/20的议题，”他说，“所以我其实很喜欢我们这里的胜算……我们会超出预期。参议院，我们会守住。众议院会是一场恶战，但我看好我们的机会。”他甚至预言了就是这一周，告诉我该党将“看到他的信息传递发生变化，并在达拉斯的中期选举大会上重置”，此后“你会看到那些数字开始变化”。达拉斯究竟是否真的带来了那种重置——还是只带来了一笔5000美元的贿赂和一个处于守势的特朗普——往好里说，也是个未解之谜。而出席名单表明，皮尔逊自己党内的一些候选人并不打算留下来等答案。

##段落
4. JD·万斯的钢丝绳——有一个人无法享受与特朗普保持距离的好处，那就是JD·万斯，他是副总统，也是2028年总统提名共和党方面公认的领跑者。他与那些对特朗普已经失望的右翼声音关系密切，而且他必须操心选民的时间比总统更长久，而伊朗战争、关税以及特朗普的种种承诺，全都……

##段落
这给他带来了冲突。就在上周，他因拒绝谴责塔克·卡尔森而遭到特朗普阵营中知名人士的猛烈抨击。卡尔森是播客主持人兼前电视主播，已成为以色列政府和特朗普第二任期议程的尖锐批评者。展望他今晚的演讲，我将关注他如何处理特朗普的关税、伊朗战争和汽油价格。他试图在经济问题上比特朗普表现出更多同理心，而特朗普将可负担性危机的讨论描述为旨在政治上伤害他的编造叙事——即便属实，那也是乔·拜登总统的错。“是他们造成的，但我们在修复，”总统周三表示。万斯说，他在中期选举之后才会与特朗普“坐下来”讨论自己的2028年计划，但特朗普似乎不是那种会给继任者留出很大空间来撇清自己记录的人。本周我与《康科德箴言报》记者夏洛特·马瑟利交谈，她一直在跟踪报道被低估的新罕布什尔州参议院选举。新罕布什尔州是民主党夺回参议院必须拿下的州之一，但有人担心共和党候选人约翰·苏努努——一位在新罕布什尔州拥有深厚家族传承的前参议员——可能会给民主党提名人、众议员克里斯·帕帕斯带来严重麻烦。我与马瑟利讨论了该州初选的教训以及大选的预期。

##段落
那么，新罕布什尔州初选刚刚结束——有哪些看点？为什么这场选举一直未受关注？随着进步派与温和派的对话在全国展开，这是我进入周二时的最大疑问。我们这里是否也会看到那波进步浪潮或涟漪，或者随便你怎么称呼它？因为我们确实有一位进步派候选人[卡里什玛·曼祖尔]与克里斯·帕帕斯竞争，她真正聚焦于人道主义，并致力于终结她所认为的美国对外国战争的共谋。喜欢她的选民对她非常热情，但最终，我认为人们只是想投票给他们熟悉的人，而[帕帕斯]已经在国会任职了。我们在全国看到的进步浪潮未必在这里得到了体现。你认为为什么新罕布什尔州与全国进步浪潮保持距离？

##段落
为了给你提供新罕布什尔州政治的语境，它总是与全国选民有些不同。我们是一个真正的紫色州——独立选民是这里最大的投票群体。但也有一些奇特之处。比如，过去20年来，除了少数例外，选民倾向于把共和党人送进州议会，但在国会或总统选举中通常投票给民主党。所以在这里分裂投票非常普遍。每次我出去采访，都会听到人们说……

##段落
要判断过去几年里有人转投了哪个党派，或者他们是否来回摇摆，民调很难说清。所以在这里，党派界线究竟划在哪里，实在很难判断。共和党候选人约翰·苏努努是如何应对唐纳德·特朗普的受欢迎程度的？几年前[2024年]，苏努努实际上撰写了一篇专栏文章，称唐纳德·特朗普是“失败者”。党内对此颇有微词。但特朗普最终 actually 支持了他，他还获得了实力雄厚的筹款人以及许多希望将该席位翻红的保守派组织的支持。尽管如此，苏努努仍在试图强调自己独立于本届政府。他说他不担心讨好谁之类的事，但他并没有在自己和特朗普之间拉开太多政策分歧。我能想到的一个例子是，他说他反对特朗普与伊朗协议中[据报道3000亿美元]用于重建的款项。他曾表示，他认为美国不应为重建提供任何资金。所以，诸如此类的一些事情，他试图与总统保持一定距离。

##段落

readings.title: 'Brutal' toll of war on Dubai's tourist trade
body: 2 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sameer Hashmi Last year Dubai welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally, but the US-Israel war with Iran has had a devastating impact on visitor numbers, and local businesses are struggling. On most evenings, Dubai's restaurants would usually be packed, with the constant buzz of diners, of tourists and residents filling tables across the city. But over the past month, many of those tables have sat empty. For Natasha Sideris, the shift has been sudden and stark. She opened her first restaurant in Dubai in 2014. Over the past decade, her Tashas hospitality group has grown to 14 outlets across the country, employing more than 1,000 people. But the US-Israel war with Iran is now taking a heavy toll on her business. Sideris says many of her restaurants, which are popular with both residents and expats, have seen revenues fall by more than 50%. But outlets that depend heavily on tourists have been hit much harder, with declines of 70% to 80%. The crisis has forced her to cut salaries by 30% for all staff including herself. "The current situation is brutal," she says. "I had a choice – either fire 30% of my staff or cut salaries to save jobs. I chose the latter for now." Sideris adds that the impact would have been worse if many of her outlets were not located inside community malls and close to residential neighbourhoods, where they still rely on local customers. The current tough reality is playing out across much of Dubai's restaurant sector. One senior executive at a restaurant chain, who asked not to be named, said footfall at its outlets has dropped to just 15-20% of normal, forcing them to place more than half of staff on unpaid leave. "We have no option," he says. "We've already shut down a few outlets temporarily, and the rest are operating with minimal staff." The impact is not limited to restaurants. The entire tourism ecosystem – from hotels and travel agencies, to transport companies and airlines – is feeling the strain. Over the past two decades, Dubai has built itself into one of the world's leading tourism hubs. Last year, the emirate welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally. But since the war began, that momentum has been sharply disrupted. The wider UAE has come under repeated attacks, with Dubai among the key targets of Iran's military response following US and Israeli strikes. Authorities say more than 2,400 missiles and drones have been launched towards the UAE, targeting airports, ports and civilian areas, including hotels and residential buildings. More than 90% of them were intercepted and destroyed, officials say. But some debris has fallen across parts of Dubai, including major residential areas, hotels and the airport. Images of fragments striking the Fairmont hotel on the upscale Palm Island were circulated widely online. To date, 11 people have been killed and more than 185 injured across the UAE, according to authorities in the country. The conflict, which began on 28 February, has disrupted air travel across the region. In the early weeks, tens of thousands of visitors were stranded before being evacuated on special flights. Thousands of regular, scheduled flights have been cancelled since the conflict began, bringing one of the region's busiest travel hubs to a halt at times. Dubai International Airport – the world's busiest for international passengers – handled 95.2 million travellers last year.  Some operations have since resumed, with flag-carrier Emirates operating a reduced flight schedule while working to restore full network operations. But with tourists leaving and the number of new arrivals collapsing, hotel stays in Dubai have fallen steeply. Occupancy levels across Dubai hotels dropped to between 15% and 20% of the usual level for this time of the year in the weeks following the outbreak of the war, according to Mamoun Hmiden, chief business officer at travel booking firm Wego. Hotels have responded with deep discounts, particularly during the Eid period, in an attempt to attract residents. Some luxury properties on Palm Jumeirah, one of the city's premium hotel hubs, have cut prices by as much as half. "The uncertainty is disrupting everyone at the moment," says Hmiden. Some hospitality chains have temporarily shut down some properties or closed certain sections, citing scheduled renovations – a move typically seen during the quieter summer months. A senior executive at an international hospitality group said occupancy at some properties had fallen to single digits. "It made sense to cut operational costs by shutting down for a few weeks and reviewing the situation later," he says. Even business hotels are under pressure. Dubai, a major hub for conferences and events, has seen organisers cancel or postpone large gatherings in the coming months. Majestic Hotels, which operates around 450 rooms across three properties, says occupancy has dropped to record lows. "We are seeing cancellations beyond April," says Varun Raj, cluster director of sales and marketing. "A lot of events have been cancelled, making it difficult for travellers to plan ahead." The slowdown comes after several years of rapid growth. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Dubai was among the first destinations to reopen to international visitors, allowing its tourism sector to recover faster than many global peers. Since then, it has expanded into a broader and more diversified market – strengthening its position as a luxury destination, while also attracting large numbers of mid-market and price-sensitive travellers from regions such as South Asia, Europe and the former Soviet states. That surge in demand has been matched by a sharp increase in supply. Years of growth have driven expansion not only in hotel capacity, but also in short-term apartment rentals across the city. That additional supply is now under pressure. Data firm AirDNA shared that a little over 226,500 short-term bookings were cancelled across the UAE between February 28 to March 29, the first month since the war began.   The downturn is also being felt by the migrant workforce that form the backbone of Dubai's hospitality industry – from restaurant staff to hotel workers.  As demand weakens, many have seen their hours reduced, or they have been placed on unpaid leave. While the UAE's labour system allows companies to adjust quickly to changing conditions, that flexibility can leave workers exposed to sudden income losses. "It feels like we are back to the Covid-19 period," says a South Asian waiter working at a high-end restaurant. There are fears we could lose our jobs again and be forced to go back home." He and several colleagues have been placed on unpaid leave, with no clarity on when – or if – they will return to work. Some hotels, including five-star properties, have started laying off employees. Rights groups say many migrant workers in the UAE are already financially vulnerable, with some carrying debt linked to recruitment fees. The impact of the war is also being felt across the wider Middle East. Research by Tourism Economics, part of Oxford Economics, suggests that between 23 million and 38 million fewer people could travel to the region this year, depending on how long the conflict continues. Between $34bn (£25bn) and $56bn in visitor spending could be lost. "If the war ends soon, there could be a quick recovery," says Hmiden. "But if it drags on, we have to start questioning the entire summer season." This week – Dubai announced $272.26 million in support for businesses, including tourism, over the next three to six months. Hotels will be allowed to delay sales-related fees and tourism dirham charges – a fee applied to guests staying in the city.  Authorities in Dubai are also working on plans to revive tourism once the conflict subsides, including new campaigns and promotional offers.  "The war is out of our control," says one official. "But we are preparing for when it ends." More like this: • How the Iran war is affecting global travel • How a prolonged Middle East conflict could reshape how we fly • Is Dubai's glossy image under threat? Sideris is hoping that landlords will provide rent relief in the form of deferred payments or reduced payments for the time being to support local businesses. For Sideris, the outlook remains uncertain. She says a recovery is possible from October if the war ends soon. But if the conflict continues, the timeline could shift to next year – bringing the risk of layoffs and outlet closures. "We've got enough cash to see us through a month or two... maximum three, and then past that, what do we do? After that, we will have to take tougher calls. Hopefully not. And this insanity ends soon." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights.
